utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We'll first establish that the accused are not there. We discussed this yesterday. I don't think that we have received any waiver forms, but since they expressed themselves clearly yesterday in court, we'll proceed in their absence. I'd like to continue where we left off yesterday. The next item on my agenda relates to P117. There was some discussion as to whether P117, photographs discussed in the statement of Witness JF-007, whether that is a public document or confidential document. Until now, it has been qualified as confidential, but that seems to be a mistake. Mr. Hoffmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's correct. We submit it could be made public. It's a photo collection, and there's no reference to the witness or nothing else that would identify the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P117 will be a public document. The Chamber decides that it will change its status from confidential into public. Then we had a question about the status, that is, confidential or public, also in relation to documents which were admitted through Witness JF-006. I think we said in court that we didn't have to discuss the matter in court, but that the parties would discuss among themselves to what extent these documents could be made public. We have not received any response from the parties in this respect, from my recollection. I don't know who to address. Mr. Hoffmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wasn't present at that session, myself, but my information from my team is that Exhibits P106, P107, and P108 could, in fact, be changed to public status.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is this the outcome of a consultation with the Defence, because if I read what I said, that I would suggest that you discuss with the Defence whether there are any without in any way making the protective measures ineffective could become public. Did you express a joint position, or was it the OTP position?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I'm afraid at this point that's only the OTP position. I think, if I recollect, the discussion was about one of the Defence exhibits, and in the course of that discussion, just to be on the safe side, the other documents were kept under seal. But that discussion was mainly about Exhibit D7, if I recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Defence, first in relation to the P exhibits and then in relation to the D exhibit just mentioned. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honours, in relation to the P exhibits, then we would simply go along with the Prosecution's position, they having checked the protective measures issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say it's their witness, so they should be primarily concerned about any protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. May I just take a moment for the Exhibit D7 just to check that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, D7 will -- it might be that we have a short break at a later stage and that we deal with any matter which is still pending. Mr. Hoffmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I would ask that we quickly go into private session for this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then I would repeat in open session that a number has been assigned to the unredacted statement of Witness Kozarcanin, P259, which is admitted under seal. I move on to a few outstanding requests for a change of page limits and requests for reply. I have to take you back in history, because these matters are pending since 2007, at a time, I think, that none of us was yet on this Chamber. For transparency, the Chamber still needs to decide on two outstanding requests, both the -- and that's the first one, 9th of July, 2007, Stanisic Defence request for leave to exceed the page limit in its response to Prosecution motions for admission of written evidence, pursuant to Rule 92 ter, and - and I now come to the second - the 16th of July, 2007, Prosecution request for leave to reply to Defence responses to Prosecution motions pursuant to Rule 92 ter. Both these requests are granted. The next item. The Chamber would like to put on the record some informal communications which should be on the record. The Chamber hereby puts on the record that on the 14th of July, 2009, the Chamber informally denied a Prosecution request for leave to reply to the Stanisic Defence response to Prosecution motion for admission of written evidence of Witness C-058. I also put on the record that on the 18th of December, 2009, the Chamber informally indicated that the reasons underlying the objections raised by the Stanisic Defence in its Defence response to Prosecution motion for admission of written evidence of Witness JF-005, pursuant to Rule 92 ter, were considered to be insufficient to justify a denial for the Prosecution to present Witness JF-005 testimony pursuant to Rule 92 ter. So, consequently, the Chamber denied the Prosecution's request for leave to reply. The next item on my agenda deals with the e-mail that was presented by Witness JF-005. I would like to put on the record that the parties have been provided with the e-mail correspondence of Witness JF-005 on which the name and any identifying information of the witness's friend has been redacted. I also inform you that the Chamber has no intention to further follow up on this matter proprio motu. I take it that you still are aware of this, the witness sought for some material to be sent to him, material which finally was already available to the parties. I'd like to move for the next item into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, you had not identified yourself, I think, as being present in court, whereas I should have done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. Adam Weber on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. We are now back in open session, and the next item on my agenda is the letter that Mr. Stanisic has sent -- or at least the letter dates from the 7th of January and was addressed to the Chamber. First of all, the Chamber has followed up with the Registry on the matters contained in Mr. Stanisic's letter to the Chamber regarding his health situation. Both the memo of the Chamber and Dr. Eekhof's answer will be filed. And as matters stand now, the Chamber sees no reason not to be satisfied by the explanations given by Dr. Eekhof. But, of course, since you may not be fully aware of it, it's as matters stand now, and as far as the Chamber's aware. In addition to the specific subject matter of the letter, there is a general question of whether sending a letter through e-mail to Chamber staff is an appropriate way to approach the Chamber, and we'd like to inform the parties that generally we would expect counsel to put any communication from the accused into a motion or a request form and then file it with the Registry. The Chamber would also like to remind counsel and the accused, and you'll pass on this message, I take it, about the Chamber's specific judicial competencies, as opposed to the Registry's competencies, in relation to treatment and care of the accused. In exceptional circumstances, an accused could also directly address the Chamber without going through counsel. However, this could then also be done in court, rather than by way of sending a letter; of course, unless there's some very specific conflict which an accused would like to raise without counsel to know, which is really something which the Chamber would not expect at this moment to arise at all. But I can't say that it -- in the history of this institution and our sister institution, that such matters never happens, but that's really -- addressing the Chamber is already exceptional; this should be done in court, and only in extremely exceptional circumstances, and not a direct approach in another way could be considered. Are there any questions in relation to this item? There are not. Then I move on to the next item, which is guidance by the Chamber, guidance on the Prosecution's first motion for admission of exhibits from the Bar table. I hope that the booths have been provided with hard copies. On the 23rd of November, 2009 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do have the hard copies. We apologise. The interpreters were given the hard copies yesterday, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Well, if I would say something was given to me yesterday, as you just told me, I would still have to consider whether I lost it overnight. But apparently you will have an opportunity to distribute the hard copies. I'll move on, meanwhile, with other matters. I skipped two items. We'll come back to them soon. The next item on my agenda deals with the assigning of Defence exhibit numbers. The Simatovic Defence has inquired whether Defence exhibits should be given 1D or 2D rather than just D numbers. The Chamber has considered this request, but could not see why the requested system would be any better than the one so far used by this Chamber. Moreover, it is always visible on e-court whether a certain document was tendered by the Stanisic or by the Simatovic Defence. And, accordingly, this request is denied, and we will continue with the system we started with, that is, that the exhibit number expresses whether it's a P or a D exhibit that does not make any distinction between 1D or 2D. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you, and I apologise for rising. I understand your decision. My question only is whether we may retain, pending a D number -- can we actually still use the 2D prefix until when we actually propose a document for admission as an exhibit, pending its assignment of a number which would have a D prefix?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, you're referring to what I would call the 65 ter numbers, what you have there. There's no problem in using those numbers, as long as it is clear to the Registrar what you refer to. But once we decide on admission and once exhibit numbers, which is different from 65 ter numbers, once exhibit numbers will be assigned, we'll use the system of just D and nothing in addition to that identifying the party that tenders the document. Then I think I could revisit the guidance on the Prosecution's first motion for admission of exhibits from the Bar table. On the 23rd of November, 2009, the Prosecution filed its motion seeking admission of 336 exhibits from the Bar table. On the 4th of December, 2009, the Simatovic Defence partly responded to the motion and asked for additional time to respond to the remaining part. On the 8th of December, 2009, the Stanisic Defence responded to the motion. The present Bar table motion was filed at an early stage of the proceedings, and since then the Prosecution has tendered into evidence several of the documents, being part of the motion, through its witnesses. In this respect, the Chamber urges the parties to adopt an approach whereby documents are tendered through witnesses, to the extent possible. In light of this, the Chamber will not decide on the motion at this early stage of the proceedings, with the expectation that the documents can be more appropriately and efficiently be tendered through witnesses to be called during the Prosecution's case. For the sake of efficiency, the Chamber further considers that the Simatovic Defence is not expected to file a response to the motion at this stage of the proceedings. At the same time, if, at a later stage of the proceedings, the parties consider a Bar table motion to be appropriate, the parties are encouraged to file it in the form of a joint submission. Accordingly, the tendering party should file a table containing a short description of each exhibit, as well as its relevance and probative value if not immediately obvious from the description already. In case of bulky exhibits with particularly relevant portions, a reference to those portions is needed. In the joint submission, as well as in the said table of exhibits, the other parties may also provide any comments and/or objections they may have with regard to each tendered exhibit. And this concludes the Chamber's guidance on Bar table submissions. I add to this the following: When I said if at a later stage of the proceedings the parties should consider a Bar table motion to be appropriate, of course, I primarily was referring to later stages where other documents may have already been admitted. Of course, the Chamber was concerned that we receive a Bar table motion and then find at least a number of those documents already to be admitted through witnesses, so those documents should not have been Bar-tabled, but should have been introduced through witnesses. Now, there may well be a number of exhibits which cannot appropriately be introduced through witnesses, and then, of course, if that could be established most likely at a later stage, we could receive Bar table motions in the format as I just set out. Sometimes we find ourselves in a bit of a mixed situation. From other cases, I have the experience that sometimes it makes sense to introduce one or two documents through a witness and, and then if there is a series of similar documents, 10 or 20, that not to go through each and every of those documents and then to submit those in a Bar table submission and say -- and then this most likely will have been discussed in court, I have another 18, or another 25, or another 40 of these documents, and we'd like to Bar-table them. That, of course, would be -- if I said "at a later stage," we always have to consider in what situation we find ourselves. And for this first Bar table submission the Chamber was really concerned that we were offered quite a lot of documents which, I would say, almost in a natural way were later introduced through witnesses. The Chamber, therefore, will be very -- will always critically assess the situation in which documents are tendered in a Bar table motion and see whether it's appropriately done, both in terms of time and in terms of the subject matter involved. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just to explain some of the rationale underlying the written motion, it wasn't simply about choosing between doing it in written form or with the witness. It seemed to the Prosecution that it was only a fair and better efficient use of court time for the Chamber to have the documents underlying the evidence so that the Chamber could study those documents, because I would think that the Chamber's decision on admissibility may very well depend on the Chamber's assessment of the request of the correspondence that was received describing the provenance of the document, so the Prosecution considered that the better way to proceed was to put that before the Chamber, let the Chamber study those documents and come to its own view, not only with respect to the admissibility of a document but then ultimately to its weight. Now, I accept what the Chamber said with respect to guidance, and I'm thinking is there another way that we can efficiently make this correspondence available to the Chamber so that it can refer to it, so that when we do Bar-table a motion or Bar-table an exhibit into court, the Chamber has some idea about the background of how that document came into the possession of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The guidance also included a joint filing, which means that the Chamber, if looking at background or whatever, that the Chamber would not do that on the basis of the filing by one party only, but that we -- we are concerned about being flooded by hundreds and hundreds of documents of which we would not really know what to look at, precisely, what is the reason why it is presented in this way, and not knowing what the other party thinks about admissibility. Therefore, again, the Chamber is not opposed to appropriate Bar-table filings, but then would like to receive all the relevant information, and also would still prefer to receive evidence, even documentary evidence, primarily through witnesses. But as I explained before, it may well be that in this context that still it would be appropriate to Bar-table certain documents, but then we have a clear context, we know what you want, we know what the Defence response to it is, and then we can consider whether or not it is appropriate to introduce the documents in this way. And secondly, of course, we have already an indication as to whether there are any objections against admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, would the Court find it acceptance if we tendered as an exhibit -- as a single exhibit all of underlying documents with respect to documents that we intend to introduce through -- from the Bar table during the course of the trial? This way, the advocate who is tendering the exhibit could refer the Chamber to P100, for example, and page 3 of that for the underlying documentation that supports the authenticity of the document at issue in the particular tendering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If we are talking about authenticity, I can imagine that you say that the whole story of authenticity, we shouldn't raise that in court if there's no need to do that. But then, of course, if you want to introduce any underlying material -- first of all, of course, most important is whether you have discussed with the Defence whether there's any authenticity issue. And if there is an authenticity issue, then it may well be that we say, This is the document we'll use in court, and for purposes of establishing authenticity these are underlying documents, but then where to look at exactly how you got it. These sometimes are lengthy documents, there's whole lists of what is sent. Look at paragraph 3, number so-and-so, there you find the document. And then we'd also hear from the Defence whether there's any challenge to the content of that material, so that we are better able to decide. Perhaps if it would assist the parties, from other cases, of course, we have examples of how these Bar-table submissions were made. If the parties would like to be informed about how this practice developed, the Chamber staff will certainly be available to give further guidance. Then the Chamber still owes the parties the reasons for its decision to grant protective measures for Witness C-1118. The decision was delivered on the 15th of July, 2009, and the reasons will now be given. On the 14th of July, 2009, the Prosecution requested that Witness C-1118 be granted the protective measures of use of a pseudonym and testimony with face and voice distortion. On the 15th of July, 2009, before commencement of his testimony, the Chamber and the parties questioned the witness on his reasons for requesting protective measures. This can be found on transcript pages 1950 through 1957. On the same day, the Chamber decided to grant protective measures for the witness. The Chamber decided to go beyond what was requested by the Prosecution and grant the use of a pseudonym and testimony in closed session. I refer to transcript pages 1959 through 1961. And the public is hereby informed of that decision. As the Chamber has set out in previous decisions on protective measures, the party seeking protective measures for a witness must demonstrate an objectively-grounded risk to the security or welfare of the witness, or the witness's family, should it become known that the witness has given evidence before the Tribunal. This standard may be satisfied by showing that a threat was made against the witness or the witness's family. It may also be meant by demonstrating a combination of the following three factors: 1. The witness's testimony may antagonise persons who reside in a specific territory. 2. The witness, or his or her family, live or work in that territory, have property in that territory, or have concrete plans to return to live in that territory. 3. There exists an unstable security situation in that territory which is particularly unfavorable to witnesses who appear before the Tribunal. The Chamber adds to this that assessing whether or not to grant protective measures involves a delicate balance between the right of the accused to a public trial, on the one hand, and the interests and need for protection and privacy for victims or witnesses, on the other. In this respect, the Chamber is mindful that protective measures do not negatively affect an accused's other fair-trial rights, such as the right to examine witnesses against him. Even though granting protective measures is and should be the exception to the rule of a public trial, the threshold for when protective measures should be granted cannot be set too high. For example, to exclude persons who have not experienced actual threats or harassment would defy the purpose of the measures; namely, the protection from risks that might occur as a result of the testimony. The Chamber must, therefore, make a risk assessment, and inherent in such an assessment is applying a certain level of caution and erring on the safe side. Witness C-1118 is a Croatian Serb living in the same Serb-majority village in Croatia he lived in during the indictment period in the present case. His testimony concerns events occurring in the area of his village and involving many local Serbs. The witness stated that some of the people he would testify about currently live in his village. The witness believed that should it become known that he had testified, he would receive threats from his neighbours, even though he had not experienced any problems with them until that point in time. The witness added that there is a tension between Croats and Serbs in the area he lives in and that a large percentage of the local police are Serbs and were policemen already during the conflict. For these reasons, the Chamber decided to grant protective measures for Witness C-1118. The Chamber considered that in view of the subject matter of the witness's testimony, the protective measures requested by the Prosecution, namely, pseudonym and face and voice distortion, would not guarantee the witness's security. This was also acknowledged by the Prosecution and the Simatovic Defence, while the Stanisic Defence did not take a position on this matter. This can be found on transcript page 1960. Therefore, the Chamber decided, pursuant to Article 20 of the Tribunal Statute, and Rule 75 of the Tribunal's Rules, that Witness C-1118 should be referred to by his pseudonym in all public proceedings and filings, and that he should testify with the protective measures of closed session. And this concludes the reasons for the Chamber's decision. Some of the language used in the reasons for these protective measures may sound quite familiar to the parties by now, because the criteria applied by the Chamber are repeated in many decisions. The Chamber is considering, in future decisions, to make a brief reference to earlier decisions by perhaps pointing at two or three elements or the elements which we usually apply, and only give the full set of reasons if there is any deviation in this respect, which will save some time in court. I would like to move on to a matter in relation to Witness Tihic. The Prosecution has provided an informal list - I think it was on the 3rd of February - of the previous testimony and/or statements to be admitted pursuant to Rule 92 ter. In item 9, reference is made to transcript of previous testimony in the Simic case. The number of that case is mentioned, and then the transcript pages are referred to as T-1495 up to and including T-1522. In the fourth column, which is under the heading "Closed Session/Under Seal," we find "T-1516, line 16, to T-1522, line 30." The Chamber was confused by this way of presenting the evidence, especially since what was up-loaded in e-court was T-1495 up to and including T-1522, but with the lines I just mentioned, "Closed Session," being redacted. If it is indicated that those pages are part of the testimony which is submitted under Rule 92 ter, those pages are part of it, whether in closed session or not. I mean, if it's relevant evidence, closed session or not, that maybe has consequences for public or non-public versions, but the Chamber should not be confronted with redacted portions. Therefore, it was confusing. What apparently was intended is, as a matter of fact, to exclude those redacted portions, although they were included in the description of the testimony which was tendered into evidence. Now, this may not have great effect on the outcome, because the Chamber had the possibility in checking what was redacted, because the Chamber, if need be - and we'll not use that for any inappropriate reason -- the Chamber has the possibility of checking evidence even in closed session in the other cases. Again, we would not do that unless there was a good reason. Here, we did, and we found, as a matter of fact, that those five pages are dealing exclusively with procedural matters. So, first of all, they should not have been tended as evidence, because it has no probative value whatsoever; it was procedural stuff, rather than evidence. That's one. Second, it should not have been included in the testimony which was tendered, because no reason for us to read pages and pages of procedural matters. And, third, it should not have been redacted. The Chamber wants to receive any evidence unredacted for us. I mean, for the public, it may be different. This was a rather confusing thing. It took us a while to find out what exactly happened. Again, for the outcome, it's not that important, so the Chamber is not seeking at this moment any remedy to that, but wants to address the issue, because if large documents, transcripts of testimony, are tendered, we should be very precise in what we really need and what we do not need. I'll come back to that at a -- I would say at a later stage, but this was an example. I'll come back to that right away. And I'm now talking in more general terms about voluminous 92 ter submissions. Through Witness Tihic, the Prosecution tendered very voluminous prior testimony. This was further discussed in court on the 4th of February, 2010. In relation to Witness Tihic's previous testimony, before taking a final decision on admission into evidence of P176 and P177 - we, by the way, just dealt with Exhibit P176 - the Chamber strongly urges the parties to come to an agreement to reduce the size of the tendered documents by focusing on core issues as well as contextual additions. For example, if a curriculum vitae appears both in a statement and is extensively discussed in prior testimony, the Chamber is not assisted by such repetitious tendering. Similarly, many pages from prior testimony may contain less relevant aspects for this case and should be excluded from any tendering. The parties are hereby instructed to keep this guidance in mind, and more specifically for P176 and P177, are instructed to submit reduced versions by the 15th of March, 2010. For the next item, I'd like to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The next item is about the -- it's P164. On the 26th of January, Mr. Groome, the Chamber noted that the document was redacted; that is, the biography of Milan Ninkovic. The Chamber inquired into the redactions. Especially on the third page, there is a redaction. You, at that moment, thought that you would have received the document with those redactions, but you said you would check on that and report back to the Chamber in a few minutes. Within the next few minutes of the transcript, we could not find anything, but the Chamber would like to give you the opportunity to report the result of your verification.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, indeed, we have checked this document again, and it's true that we have received it as it was tendered, that is, with those redactions. We have also not found any unredacted version of the same document. Also, there is -- I think on the document you can see a web site reference, which is actually not the public web site, so we're not able at this point in time to find any unredacted version. So we have used the document as we have it. That's all we can say at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. But do you have a general explanation on the reasons for redactions of any material received from SFOR? Because if you say, Well, that's how we received it, so you have to do with that, then, of course, we would know what other criteria applied when redacting documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: The letter that we have that indicates when and how we got this document does not refer to the criteria applied by SFOR when redacting those statements -- or that document. It's our understanding that when those documents are provided, they are de-classified, and during that process they do some redactions, but we have no record of what criteria SFOR applied when applying those redactions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hoffmann, the Chamber is not used to assess the probative value of documents which are redacted by others for unknown reasons. Therefore, the Prosecution is invited to further inquire into the reasons perhaps of redactions, in general, but more specifically this document. I mean, it's not one name or something of the kind; it's a whole paragraph which is redacted. So, therefore, since the Chamber would really like to be able to not form its opinion and render judgement on the basis of selection made by others for unknown reasons, the Prosecution is invited to follow up on this redaction. And perhaps, in that context, of redactions in a more general way with SFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: We will certainly try our best, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These were the items, apart from the MFI list, which I would like to deal with now. Not all documents which are MFI'd are yet ready to be given a follow-up, but some of them are. The first one is P18, which is a BBC interview with Vojislav Seselj. Very few parts of this video were shown, and they were used with the witness to identify Mr. Seselj. Now, a considerable part of the document seems like perhaps to be Bar-tabled, but having looked at only small portions to identify Mr. Seselj, the Chamber would like to hear from the Prosecution whether you would at this point in time want to tender a reduced version. Just to get in a whole video and asking a witness, Is this Mr. Seselj, that's not a proper way of presenting evidence. Therefore, the Chamber would like to hear from you, how you would like to deal with P18.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. I think the video at the time was, in fact, tendered in addition to the three clips that were played, from the Bar table. It is still our submission that the Chamber should have in front of it the whole video. I think there are only a very few parts in the beginning that we discussed as potentially to be excluded that deal with the biography of Mr. Vojislav Seselj. The clips played were not only played to identify Vojislav Seselj, and I think on the record it is clear that there is no dispute between the parties that this video is authentic, that it is Mr. Seselj giving an interview in March 1995 to the BBC, but the Witness Savic at the time also made his own comments and testified to those clips and what was said on the clips. And the Prosecution certainly intends to use other parts of this video with upcoming witnesses, which is why we submit it would be easier for the reference if you have the video, as such, in evidence as one exhibit with the full transcripts, so when we come back to certain parts of it with other witnesses, the context is still clear and we don't end up with, let's say, maybe 10 or 20 exhibits from the same one video. At the time when this was discussed in July last year, the parties were invited to see if there's an agreement about which portions could be admitted or should be admitted. From those discussions and the follow-up correspondence, it is clear that there is no dispute about that the three clips should be tendered into evidence. We had an indication from the Stanisic Defence that they would agree to larger portions of the video, indicated by certain pages of the transcript, but the Simatovic Defence at the time finally responded that they would only agree to the admission of the three clips. So in that respect, we have to respond that there is no agreement on any other admission, apart from the three clips. But we would still tender the video, as such, from the Bar table for the reasons just given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you say, Well, it's a bit of a mixed approach, apparently, because you say, We tender it, rather not to cut it into pieces, so that if we deal with other parts of the video with future witnesses then we would have to constantly monitor what now of this whole video is dealt with through other witnesses and what is not. You're anticipating on witnesses which are still to be called and still to appear before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: If I may add, Your Honour, we would submit that it's basically the same approach that was taken with the Kula Camp video, Exhibit P61, where initially short clips were played. There was no dispute between the parties about the authenticity, no dispute about the general relevance of it. Of course, there is different interpretation of the video, but the Chamber admitted then the whole video as one exhibit. And we have used this exhibit now with different witnesses, and we haven't had the need to then tender portions and go through that process, but we simply just played different clips from the P61. And we would submit that would be, in our view, the best approach with this video as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I can imagine that the concern of the Defence would be what finally remains as not ever being played and not being dealt with by any witness. Could I hear from the Defence teams. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: At the time the video was played and shown to a particular witness, there was a very discreet part of the video which the witness was asked to comment on. Your Honours then issued a directive indicating that exhibits which are put to witnesses and tendered should be relevant to that witness's testimony. And in light of that directive, we indicated and the Simatovic team indicated to the Prosecution what we considered to be relevant from that video. And for the Simatovic team, it was the three clips. We, in the Stanisic team, went a bit wider than that, but, nonetheless, there was a general agreement about what was relevant. And what was not relevant was a good 8/10ths of that video, with not explanation as to its probative value or relevance to the case, and that's what we object to and that's what our present position is in relation to that video. It's very different to the Kula video, which the relevance is clear. There's an award ceremony indicating a unit with various remarks being made, and this case is going to be about whether those remarks were accurate and can be relied upon or whether that video, as a whole, corroborates the Prosecution case, as a whole. That is not the case with this video, the Seselj video. Mr. Seselj speaks widely and flamboyantly about a number of subjects which don't have immediate relevance to this case, we submit. Perhaps the Prosecution may in the future want to indicate that those areas are relevant, but so far through this witness they haven't indicated it, and they haven't indicated it through the Bar-table motion. And that's our position, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The Simatovic Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we fully agree with what Mr. Jordash our learned colleague has said. There is nothing that we would wish to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber will consider the matter. I move on to, not entirely unrelated but perhaps less contested, P21. That is a B-92 video-clip. The original up-loaded version had four excerpts, but only two of them are tendered. There were no objections against the two clips to be admitted into evidence. Has now the version which only two clips been up-loaded? Because if that's the case, we could then decide to admit the two clips tendered and get rid of the pollution, to say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's my understanding that that was done. But if we may just, in light of the time, just double-check over the break. If there is one, then we'll come back to you after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please double-check that over the break. Then I move on to P107. P107 is MFI'd under seal. I think that, nevertheless, we could deal with the matter in open session. But the parties are hereby informed not to say anything about this document which would make the protective measures ineffective. The issue being, in relation to P107, that the authenticity and the provenance of the document were questioned by the Simatovic and the Stanisic Defence, the OTP then provided further information as to the way in which this document, which is an official note, was obtained, and stated that it could provide the Defence with underlying documentation. I then said that we would further hear from the Defence, whether or not the disclosure of these underlying documents would remedy the objections raised by the Defence. The Chamber would like to check with the Defence whether the objections still stand after the discussions, any with the Prosecution. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I just quickly discuss with the Simatovic team. I think they led the objection, so I just want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What about doing that during the break we'll have anyhow, and then we'll hear from you after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I move on to P134, which is a video which was introduced through Witness B-1108. There were objections by the Stanisic Defence mainly on the basis that the prisoner speaking in this video refers to special police or special forces from Belgrade. The Simatovic Defence has joined in these objections, and suggested to the parties that all the contested references be redacted. And, meanwhile, the video and the transcript were MFI'd. Now, the Chamber does understand that redactions were agreed upon by the parties and that they were up-loaded. If that's the case, there seems to be no further objections against admission. And then, of course, the redactions to be understood as the video will not change, I take it, but that the Chamber, as far as the text spoken on that video, will exclusively pay attention to the portions of the text transcribed. From what I remember, it was someone speaking German, from what I remember. But that would mean that if we would follow this, that although the video is admitted into evidence, that we would ignore any spoken text which is left out -- is redacted in the transcript. I hear no objections with this approach. Under those circumstances, P134, a video with a redacted transcript, is admitted into evidence. I suggest that we first have a break. It may be that some matters arise after the break which would require another very brief pause after that. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to revisit a few matters which were left over before the break. The first one is D7, P106, P107, P108, the Defence was invited to look at it, and not just as a matter of courtesy, but to really look into the matter, whether they could be made public.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We come to the same conclusion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same conclusion. The Simatovic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We join Mr. Jordash's stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then under those circumstances, D7, P106, P107, and P108 are made public documents. Their status changes from confidential into public. If you would give me one second. From before the break, we have still pending P18, which is the video. The Chamber would like to invite the Prosecution to make a submission similar to what we discussed before the break, the Bar-table submission, that is, to set out specifically the non-played portions, what the relevance is subject by subject; then to present that to the Defence, that the Defence then can then make its comments in relation to relevance, or probative value, or whatever comments they have. And under the present circumstances, I can imagine that the Prosecution would, in respect of every portion of it, would also indicate with which witness they intend to further deal with the matter. Then we can see -- that also gives an opportunity to the Defence to see whether there is a risk that we have large portions of a video in evidence where we'll never hear any further evidence on it, or whether we find clues in the 65 ter summaries of those witnesses or in their statements which would give them confidence that nothing is lost at this moment in admitting the whole of the video, because it has practical advantages. It's clear that if we have 17 separate clips of a video in evidence, that is not very practical to work with. But a fair opportunity should be given to the Defence to express themselves in more detail, once the Prosecution has explained, in similar detail, what they expect to do with that or what could already have been done with the non-played part of the video. Therefore, it's not extremely urgent. How much time would you require to make such a submission? And then, of course -- I would say how much time would you need to prepare the submission up to it being available to the Defence to give their comments on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would aim at the end of next week to provide it to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I then expect the Defence teams to add their comments? Again, it's not full litigation, it's not full submissions, but just, We object because of this, or, We object because of that, or reference is made to a witness who doesn't appear on the 65 ter list, whatever, but short, to the point, so that we know more or less what we're talking about. Ten days after you receive that, would that do? Mr. Jordash is nodding, Yes. I see the Simatovic Defence -- well, if you would say, I would need two weeks or three weeks, we would consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would appreciate it if you could grant us two weeks for the Simatovic Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two weeks after you have received the initial table or the initial spreadsheet indicating what portions, what is the relevance, perhaps what witnesses to be -- then two weeks for the Defence to add their comments to what then could become a joint submission. P21, you would verify whether the new video had been up-loaded with only the two excerpts you were tendering?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that has been done, so that the transcripts and the video with those two clips only are up-loaded in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the number known to the Registrar? Same number as earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Yes, the same number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same number. Madam Registrar, hereby leave is granted to replace the earlier version of P21 to a new version of P21 as up-loaded by the Prosecution, and P21 is admitted into evidence. In relation to P107, Mr. Jordash, you asked to be given an opportunity to consult with the Simatovic Defence. Could I hear from -- I see Mr. Petrovic is on his feet. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will try to explain our joint position. As initiators of this objection, we stand by, regarding P27, in terms of authenticity. You probably have this document in front of you. It's a document that is unsigned, and the place where the signature should be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's have a look at the document. Could we have P27 on our screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there's maybe a typo. I thought we were talking about P107.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it was not a typo. It was my mistake. It is P107 which we'd like to have on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you allow us, we will see the English version in a moment, I hope, but I think it is already clear by just looking at the B/C/S version that this document is unsigned. In place of the signature, there is some kind of designation which does not point in any way as to who the author of this document might be, so that our objection remains. The Prosecution has informed us how it has obtained this document, and that is indisputable. The Prosecution has obtained this document via the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia, and this document was attached to a police report in the proceedings against Cedomir Bulat. In other words, it was part and portion of the initial document that was submitted in the proceedings against this person. We don't know what happened with this document afterwards, whether it was part of the indictment, and even less do we know how the Croatian authorities actually handled this document. We just know that it was attached to the police report or police complaint, and this doesn't really mean anything because of the fact that in our system there are numerous documents that are attached to the criminal complaint, so that this does not really help in any way. What we would request is that the Prosecutor provide some further evidence as to the provenance of this document. And if they do so in the course of these proceedings, we can revisit this issue. In the meantime, our position remains the same. This document should remain as an MFI'd document. This is our principal position on any such documents, a document that is unsigned. Unsigned and unclear documents do not really meet the requirements, especially in a situation where we don't know anything about its provenance, or authenticity, or authorship. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It does not meet what requirements exactly, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, primarily I mean the requirement of authenticity, but we can also discuss other aspects. As for its probative value, we could discuss that, but the first and foremost problem with this document is its authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What, then, do you exactly mean here by "authenticity"? Do you say it is -- because you said quite a lot of things in relation to this document. You said, well, it apparently was attached to a certain file. Then you say, We do not know what happened to this document afterwards. In what respect would that affect the authenticity?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I tried to explain the procedure. This document was part of the criminal report, as the initial document used in the proceedings against Cedomir Bulatovic [as interpreted]. Now, what happened with this document after that, whether it ever became part of an indictment, or how it was assessed by a Trial Chamber, if indeed this was brought to court, we don't know any of that. And the initial document, in its nature, is such that it consists of a huge number of documents that can later be accepted by a Trial Chamber or not. So the fact, itself, that it was part of this initial document does not really speak to its validity or to its probative value, because there are all sorts of documents that may find their way into this initial act. What later happened, we don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the way whether this document was used in those proceedings, whether it was used as evidence supporting whatever decision, seems not to be an authenticity issue. It is -- as far as I understand, you are saying that it is an authenticity issue, whereas in your explanation it appears to be a kind of a mixture of probative value, validity -- I do not know how to exactly understand what that means, whether -- I mean, the fact that it could or could not be used in local proceedings is not, in itself, an authenticity issue. It may be an aspect of weight to be given to a document. And if too little weight can be given to a document, that might come down to lack of sufficient probative value to admit it. I mean, you are mixing up a lot of matters which you then say, Well, it's primarily an authenticity issue. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I tried, when I spoke about the future destiny of this document, indicate the explanation offered by the Prosecution does not support any assertion on its authenticity. It's being part of a criminal report doesn't say anything about its authenticity. Anyone could have typed it and attached it to this criminal report. This is what I wanted to say. The very fact that it was attached to the criminal report means nothing. It doesn't say anything about this document really being drafted, but we don't know who drafted it, under what circumstances, and where. If that was not clear, I apologise for not being precise enough. All we know is that this was originally part of a criminal case file, but it doesn't offer sufficient ground for us to conclude that this was an authentic document. It could have been typed by anyone and then inserted into the case file. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which might make it an authentic document of someone unknown having typed a certain document. I mean, it's not a -- of course, the issue is whether the official status -- how we would have to establish that, if that is at all important. Perhaps it has no sufficient status. I mean, if I have a handwritten piece of paper, then it could still be authentic. It depends on what it claims to be. And if you say, This is claimed -- well, as you say, to be a judgement, but it's a forgery, because never such a judgement was passed, or, It is not signed and any judgement would have to be signed, and, therefore, there are many aspects. I would say authenticity is primarily a matter of: Is the document what it claims to be? Now, Mr. Hoffmann, there you may have a problem, because if you say it is a document which doesn't claim any more than to be a document which was in the initial file, author unknown, so no possibility whatsoever to verify that, then, of course, you might have a problem; perhaps not with the authenticity, but relevance and probative -- perhaps even not relevance, but probative value. Mr. Hoffmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Maybe just for the record, the document -- the underlying document we talk about, I just want to note for the record that this is ERN 0152-7750 in the English, the starting page. What we have provided yesterday to the parties and the Chamber is a document index which was provided by the Karlovac police. It does list this particular document, P107, which is to be found on page 2 of this document under item 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can I stop you there. The issue, apparently, is not whether you received it from the authorities. The issue, apparently, is that this was a piece of paper which ended up in a criminal file, not knowing where it comes from, not knowing what it led to, and, therefore -- again, I'm having some problems with the primary claim of authenticity, but the Chamber will consider that, whether we would require further authentication of this document. But that seems to be the problem, whereas your response at least started with explaining where it comes from.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just wanted to introduce where I'm going. It says here directly that this document, as we see it on the screen, is signed with a code-name, and in this document that we provided yesterday, it explains exactly who the author is, who is behind that code-name. It said "Code-name 91/020," in brackets "explained code for the member of DB late Djuro Ogrizovic," O-g-r-i-z-o-v-i-c, "nickname, Snjaka." So in our submission, with this document we show, A, that we got this document from the Karlovac police. I do agree that whether or not it was then used in criminal proceedings, Karlovac, to me, or to us, doesn't make any point. And, furthermore, this document shows who the author of this document is. That would be our submission. We're happy to tender this additional document if that is of assistance, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I, therefore, do understand that you rely implicitly on a practice where documents of this kind were not signed by the authors, but which were, I would say, quasi-signed by just putting the number of the relevant agent which took the statement at the bottom of the statement. Do you have any examples of similar practice, I mean, because the Simatovic Defence heavily relies on the absence of a signature? You say this was created in a system where it was not signatures, but numbers. Are similar documents known which would support your position that this actually was the way in which they made such statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I think it is our understanding that it's common practice in the intelligence. And as an example, I think we've seen a number of documents from the so-called Pauk operation. Some of them we still want to introduce at some stage, but some of them are actually only signed with a nickname of persons or only with TG-2, 3, or 1, tactical group, and without further reference, so, yes, we do have a number of those examples. And I am just been told that we also have number references, which are actually relating to Arkan, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Petrovic, on the basis of this further explanation, any further submissions to be made?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just two brief things. This document may be admissible with this additional explanation as regards authenticity. However, what my colleague says about the content of this information provided by the Croatian MUP, there is no cited source. And on what basis do they interpret that this number, "91020," can be linked to any particular individual? I can't discern that from this document. If you allow me just one more sentence, please. My colleague mentioned, for example, Tactical Group. Once you say "Tactical Group," it's very clear who the author can be. But if you have a five-digit number on an official note, drafted by an individual, without any additional evidence, does not offer any insight into the authorship of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I add to Mr. -- to the Simatovic's submissions. In our submission, simply saying that there's a code number on it and there's also a code number on other documents doesn't take the matter any further. It simply says -- it could simply say that the person who manufactured the document copied previous practice. What would, in our submission, take the matter further would be some indication as to who said it was an official note. Did the Prosecution ask somebody to confirm it was an official note? Did a named person confirm it was an official note? And, further, where did the information come as to the code number, and who can confirm the code number relates to the said DB member? It's that kind of information which would take the matter further than just simply saying it's an official note, which is all we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you studied the underlying material which apparently was available to the Prosecution and which was made available to the Simatovic Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know exactly what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's a letter, it seems, from the Republic of Croatia MUP, dated the 28th of February, without a year, and it simply lists --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it will be from next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. It simply lists the documentation that was sent from the MUP to the Prosecution. So it takes the matter no further, I think, than simply the Prosecution saying, Can you confirm you sent us the information?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But apparently with information about who was known by the person who wrote that letter -- or by the institution that wrote that letter, who was known under number 91/020.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, it says, in relation to that, official note on participation in the attack of -- when purporting to describe this exhibit or potential exhibit, official note on participation in the attack of Subosko [phoen] on the 12th of November, 1991, signed by code number 91/020 "(code for the member of the DB late Djuro Ogrizovic, nicknamed Snjaka)." And then 4.1 biography Djuro Ogrizovic. So it's simply somebody purporting to describe what we can all see. I could give the same description to the Court by looking at the document, but I have absolutely no information about the authenticity of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, you couldn't give the name of the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, but I could say, Here's the code. I say the code relates to Franko Simatovic, and no one would know any different if I simply asserted that to be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. Mr. Hoffmann, anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Just a quick note. In the original, we do find the year. It's 28 February of 2001, when this letter was sent to the ICTY. It's coming from the Republic of Croatia, the Ministry of Interior, Police Administration, Karlovac. It does say on the English document, in fact on the top of it, This document index was provided by Ivan Horvat from the Karlovac police. So we do claim that this is, at this point in time, sufficient information about the authenticity of the document. We would tender this document into evidence as underlying material, if need be. In the next step, we could only call this person who signed the letter or who provided the material. It's clearly our understanding, when this material was provided to us, that, in their understanding, they did not provide false material but what they believe are authentic documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But that, of course, is an assumption. If we would apply that, that our work might be far easier in many courts, not only in this court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: All I'm saying is I think we apply some of the standards when it comes to documents that are provided through official channels, through official correspondence, upon RFAs. I think it's not the practice that we always ask the person who's responding on an RFA to appear in court to explain that he actually provided authentic documents or documents they have found in their collection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hoffmann, the Chamber would like you to tender the document you just mentioned. A number could be assigned to it immediately. We'll MFI it, and the Chamber will take a decision on admissibility on the two documents together; that, of course, the supporting document is -- the relevance only is to see whether the claim of non-authenticity is with merits and whether the Chamber should ask, as the Chamber can do, for further authentication of the document. Could you please give the 65 ter number, if there is any yet. If not, it may not be in your 65 ter list. But since the Chamber asked you to produce it, perhaps you --

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: What I can give is the ERN again. The starting ERN is 0152-7750.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it is a letter --

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: From the Karlovac police in Croatia, dated 28 February 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 2001. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will become Exhibit P260, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And it will keep that status for the time being. I will move on. But before I move to my next MFI, I'd like to move to an MFI which isn't an MFI, it's: "What you see is not what you get." When we were looking at the associated exhibits for JF-008, Ms. Friedman said that there were two MFIs on that list. I'm talking -- two MFIs on that list. Then I corrected her and said, I see three MFIs, and she said, I stand corrected. Now, the three MFIs I saw on that list was P150, P146, and P148. Now, it turns out that where I saw three, there actually were only two, because P146, which appears on this list as an MFI, was already admitted into evidence on the 20th of January. And, therefore, Ms. Friedman was right, that there were only two MFIs, I was right that I saw three, and that is now clear on the record. So, therefore, the MFI P146 is not an MFI. Then I move on. P179 is a document which is MFI'd under seal. There are two objections against this document. The first one was the link between the witness and the document, speculation as to the identity of a person mentioned in this document. That objection is denied. Now, there was another objection. That was authenticity. It was a document which did not bear a full signature, but rather a kind of initials. And I think it was contested that this was signed by Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, but if I could inform you that based on our communications with the Government of Serbia, this is a document that they intend to file protective measures regarding, so perhaps it might be more prudent to be in private session to talk about it in detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, I would not go into any further detail on the matter. The challenge to the authenticity, the Chamber invites the Stanisic Defence to further elaborate on this challenge to authenticity. That could be done by showing that, for example, initials and signature are always different. Of course, it doesn't make that much sense to compare initials with full signatures, if documents exist both with full signature and with initials, and then to say that the initial is different from a signature, of course, it is not very helpful for the Chamber to assess the authenticity. If, however, there are other documents in your possession - but in response, of course, the Prosecution could claim that they have such documents - where you'd see that, if initialled, those initials look quite different from what we see on this document, then we have a further substantiation of the challenge of authenticity. Further, one could look at the similarity of documents, are there documents of a similar structure, similar subject matter, similar provenance, similar numbering, whatever, which are initialled where it's not contested that the initials or the signature are from Mr. Stanisic, that might help us in better understanding the challenge. And if there's any other piece of information which would shed additional light on the challenge to the authenticity, then, of course, the Chamber would like to hear that. I think best to be done in a written submission, further elaborating on the challenge of authenticity. We'd then receive the response by the Prosecution, and then the Chamber will decide whether or not it requires further proof of authenticity. As you may know, the Chamber can require such evidence. But we'd like to receive further information before coming to any conclusions in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I just inform the Court of this, because it might affect whether Your Honours still require us to do something in written form at this stage: They'll be essentially two challenges. One will be to the nature of Mr. Stanisic's job, and we will submit that his job did not entail this type of work. That's the first way which we intend to deal with it during our Defence case. And then, secondly, we will be giving due consideration to a handwriting expert. We do not know whether there is sufficient writing to conduct such analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the original available?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That, we don't know. We haven't as yet --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because I know from my experience that don't ask an expert to give an expert opinion on copies, because the first answer you'll get, that someone needs the original. But perhaps -- Mr. Jordash, have you finished or --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. It's those two ways in which we will seek to demonstrate that this document is not an authentic document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the first argument you used, that it is not within, let's say, the job description of Mr. Stanisic, to say it briefly, is of a different kind -- of a totally different kind from the second one. Now, of course, to challenge all that, there's no need to do that if the document is not admitted into evidence. So the first decision the Chamber will have to take is whether or not at this moment it would require further authenticity, and it would like to receive as much information -- of course, if you would, in this context, want to provide an expert report, we would consider that, because we asked for any information which could shed further light on the authenticity. But as I said before, there are many elements, the structure of the document, similar documents, but if you say they are not similar documents, then that would certainly support your first argument that this is not within the job description. If, however, there are 10 or 20 of the same, where there's no challenge to the signature or to the initials, then, of course, it may, to some extent, undermine your first argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. On the other hand, we -- yes, that's right. There aren't a huge number. Off the top of my head, I don't know. I think there are at least one or two more documents like this. But there are not a huge number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll have -- the Chamber invites the parties -- invites, first of all, you to make further submissions to substantiate your authenticity challenges, and if you want to include there the job description, I must admit that I don't know whether I'm the only one in this courtroom, but I have done, at some occasions, things which did not fit for the full 100 per cent in my job description in many capacities. So therefore it is a different kind of argument because it is a relative argument rather than the other part of your submission, that is, you want to have expert opinion on whether this could have been written by a certain person. You're invited to make these submissions. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll rely on written submissions as well. I would just point out now at this stage that this is a document that we received in response to a request for assistance from the Government of Serbia, number 1382, and is discussed in detail in the first Bar table motion. But we will respond to the specific submissions of Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we'll then certainly have a look at the Bar table motion. There's no need to copy everything again. Yes, I would like to close this one. Mr. Jordash, when do you think you could make submissions? I could imagine that an expert report would take more time, but just to elaborate on your challenge of the authenticity.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If we could have 14 days that would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fourteen days is granted. And then may I take it that the Prosecution, wether or not by brief references also to other submissions already made, one week, would that do?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And just if it assists Mr. Jordash, I believe the originals of the documents do exist in BIA, the new name of the former State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I would like to move on to D3, which is an official note which was introduced through Witness Saric, and the OTP contests the authenticity. The parties will be given a further opportunity to make submissions on the admission of this document, on the sources on the basis of which the OTP contested the authenticity, so we would like to receive a further elaboration on the objections. And then, of course, the Defence will have an opportunity to respond to that, so that we'll finally be able to see whether we need to order the parties to provide further evidence, as far as the authenticity is concerned. Mr. Hoffmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I was just wondering, I think it's a pretty straightforward issue with this document, and it could be dealt, I think, very shortly for all submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time do you think you would need to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Well, my submission would be probably just a few lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A few lines. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The document we're talking about is allegedly a witness statement of a certain Emil Cakalic. What this Cakalic allegedly said was put to the witness, which is fine, but then the alleged statement was tendered into evidence and marked for identification. At the time, there was no foundation laid. Witness Savic did not confirm any of the content of that statement. We submit it should be up to the Defence, if they want to call in their case this witness, they could do so. Otherwise, they could tender the statement under 92 ter. And more importantly, we noted already at the time that the same witness of whose that statement allegedly is testified under oath in the Milosevic case on the same point that was put to Witness Savic, and on three or four occasions in the Milosevic trial, and that's on 16 July 2003, he denied those very allegations, and it was just about the question whether or not Witness Savic did beat this Mr. Cakalic, yes or no. That's contained in the statement. That was put to the witness, and under oath various times in the Milosevic trial, he said that was not the case, it was not true. So we see no basis whatsoever to tender this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least to have it admitted, because it has been tendered already, isn't it? It has been MFI'd?

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Yes. No basis for admission, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Petrovic, because it was the a Simatovic Defence matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it happened while the other Defence team was here. I think that my colleague from the Prosecution is misrepresenting the context in which this statement was put to the witness. At pages 1913 and 1914, that's what was done. The main issue was whether Witness Savic questioned Witness Cakalic or not. That was the question. Do I understand the transcript? And since Witness Savic denied having interrogated Cakalic in any way, then my colleague Jovanovic tendered this statement, and this statement was shown to the witness. And this is where it all ended. It was -- the court was about to adjourn, and there was no debate. Let me remind you of one other thing. The point is not whether he had beat him or whether -- the point is whether he had questioned Cakalic. At page 24522 through 24525 in the Milosevic trial, it is my understanding that Witness Cakalic did not deny that he had been questioned by Witness Savic, and Goran Hadzic, to boot. The point is whether he questioned him, not whether he beat him. So the witness accepted the claim that he had been questioned, but not that he had been beaten. So it's not the issue of physical abuse, but of interrogation. So in this context, where Witness Savic denied having taken part in Cakalic's interrogation, my colleague Mr. Jovanovic showed him a document, which we have now in front of us, D3, and it's a document that a few days before that, on the 12th of May, 2009, was submitted to the Simatovic Defence by the Prosecution as exculpatory material under Rule 68, although there is not a clear distinction whether it was under Rule 68(1) or 68(2), but this was stated in the cover letter from the Prosecution. This is how the Defence obtained this letter. So this is the context. And given this context, there is every reason for this statement to be admitted into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if I understand you well, the Prosecution is objecting because it says that the content of the statement in the Official Note is contradicted by testimony given under oath, whereas the Simatovic Defence says that, That's not the issue for us. For us the issue is that Mr. Savic says that he never interviewed Mr. Cakalic, and this document shows that he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the main objection is the way how to introduce statements of other witnesses. It wasn't about whether or not this could be put in questions to the witness, but whether or not it's proper. And I think we've had many similar discussions before that, whether or not it's simple, without any 92 ter or bis foundation, to tender a statement of a different witness. It's up to the Defence to call Mr. Cakalic in their case, if they want. It's been put to the witness. And whether or not -- the issue is whether he was interrogated or beaten, the under-oath testimony shows that, at least in part, the statement put forward as D3 exhibit is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's still to be established, what is correct or not correct. They're contradicting. That's how I understand your observation. Mr. Hoffmann, isn't it true that Rule 92 ter applies certainly to any document which was created for the purposes of this Tribunal, whereas official notes are usually not documents which are prepared for being used in this Tribunal, and that statements prepared for other purposes can be admitted under Rule 89? I'm just asking you. It's a legal issue. You raised the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Yeah, I think you're right on this, that if we have a local statement which was not prepared primarily for the proceedings in this Tribunal, then that could be potentially admitted under 89(F). But, again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which means that your reliance on the requirements of 92 ter not to be met is, to say the least, not the most solid one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: Well, I think the issue remains that part of the statement that is put to us has been contradicted by this witness when he testified before this Tribunal under oath, so we do have an issue. And I think that the least we would say is if that statement would be admitted into evidence, then at least the corresponding Milosevic transcript should be admitted as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, would you have any objection against the Milosevic transcript to be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is absolutely acceptable to us for the pages that I've just quoted to you to be admitted into evidence and to be part of the record side by side with this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HOFFMANN
utterances.text: I would have to verify the page numbers, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would then suggest the following: that the parties are invited to sit together and to see whether the objection by the Prosecution would still stand if certain portions of the evidence of this witness, a selected portion - we're not seeking the whole of it; it's apparently focusing on a certain matter - would be admitted in relation to this document. We'd like to hear from the parties within a week. Then next one, D5. There was a request. It was an interview. It was tendered by the Stanisic Defence, and the OTP would like to have redactions of sensitive information in this document. I do know that we have a redacted version in evidence.
